title: Sorting networks: one trace, every binary input
attribution: Original lesson and authored examples for RecallWeave. Mathematical background: Sariel Har-Peled, Sorting Networks (2018), §§24.2–24.3, https://sarielhp.org/teach/notes/algos/files/24_sortnet.pdf. No source prose or diagrams copied.
license: Original lesson text and examples: CC0-1.0. Referenced works retain their own terms.

items.prompt: A comparator joins wires 1 and 3. Their incoming values are 7 and -2; wire 2 holds 5. What is the full vector after that comparator?
items.explanation: Only the joined wires change: wire 1 receives min(7, -2), wire 3 receives max(7, -2), and wire 2 stays 5.
items.transfer: Write the result for a different pair of nonadjacent wires.

items.prompt: A comparator receives 4 on both of its wires. Under this lab's strict swap rule, what should the trace record?
options: The comparator is skipped and no trace row is kept.
A trace row is kept, both values stay 4, and swapped is false.
The values change because every comparator must swap.
items.explanation: Every listed comparator executes and produces a row. Equal inputs already meet the required order, so no strict greater-than swap occurs.
items.transfer: Explain why a no-swap step still belongs in the trace.

items.prompt: Start with [3, 1, 2]. Run comparators (1,2), then (2,3), then (1,2). Which sequence lists the three after-vectors?
items.explanation: The first comparator exchanges 3 and 1. The second exchanges 3 and 2. The last compares 1 and 2 and leaves them alone; that unchanged step is retained.
items.transfer: Trace the same fixed pairs on [2, 2, -1].

items.prompt: Which procedure is a fixed comparator network?
options: After seeing the values, choose whichever pair currently looks most out of order.
Always compare (1,2), (2,3), (1,2), in that order, whatever values arrive.
Sort the input by calling an unspecified library function.
items.explanation: The pair sequence of a comparator network is fixed before it sees the data. Swap decisions depend on values, but the next wire pair does not.
items.transfer: Distinguish a value-dependent swap from a value-dependent choice of the next pair.

items.prompt: On [2,4,1,3], run (1,2), (3,4), (1,3), (2,4). The output is [1,3,2,4]. What does this establish?
options: The network sorts because the first and last values are correct.
The network fails to sort all inputs: 3 remains before 2.
The input is outside the model because it contains four distinct numbers.
items.explanation: A sorted vector must be nondecreasing at every adjacent pair. The middle inversion is a concrete counterexample to the universal sorting claim.
items.transfer: Identify one extra comparator that fixes this output; then explain why fixing one output alone is not a general proof.

items.prompt: Apply one additional comparator (2,3) to [1,3,2,4]. What is the result, and what has this single computation established?
options: [1,2,3,4]; it establishes success for this input, not by itself for every input.
[1,2,3,4]; it proves that every possible four-wire network sorts.
[1,3,2,4]; nonadjacent values cannot move.
items.explanation: The extra comparator exchanges the middle values. This is a local computation on one input; a universal claim still needs a complete argument or the applicable exhaustive binary test.
items.transfer: Try the repaired fixed sequence on another input before checking its full binary table.

items.prompt: How many distinct binary input vectors must a six-wire network sort for a complete zero–one check?
items.explanation: Each of six labeled wires independently carries 0 or 1, giving 2^6 = 64 complete inputs. Testing only six single-one inputs omits many arrangements.
items.transfer: Count the binary vectors for two, three and four wires.

items.prompt: A four-wire network's complete 16-row binary table contains one output [0,1,0,1]. What conclusion is justified?
options: The network is certified because it passed most rows.
The network is not a sorting network; this row is an unsorted binary witness.
The row should be discarded because its input has repeated values.
items.explanation: The adjacent 1,0 is out of order. A single counterexample defeats a claim about every input, even when all other rows pass.
items.transfer: Read the failing input as well as the output, and trace where the inversion survives.

items.prompt: An output has 7 before 4. Map every value x to 0 when x ≤ 4 and to 1 when x > 4. What happens to this out-of-order pair?
options: It becomes 0 before 1.
It becomes 1 before 0.
Both values become 0.
items.explanation: The larger value 7 maps to 1 and 4 maps to 0, so the inversion remains visible in binary form. The same fixed map must be applied to the entire input.
items.transfer: Choose a threshold for a different strict inversion.

items.prompt: Why can the same threshold map be moved through each min/max comparator in the zero–one argument?
options: The threshold map preserves weak order, so mapping min/max agrees with taking min/max after mapping.
Threshold maps make all input values distinct.
A comparator may choose a different pair after the values are mapped.
items.explanation: A nondecreasing threshold map can merge equal-side values but cannot reverse their order. It therefore commutes with min and max. Applying this fact at every fixed comparator links the mapped input to the mapped output.
items.transfer: Check the commuting identity once when the two values are on the same side of the threshold and once when they are on opposite sides.

items.prompt: A fixed min/max network passes every binary input of its wire count. What follows from the zero–one principle?
options: It sorts all vectors of ordered values of that length under the same comparison order.
It has the fewest possible comparators.
It preserves the original identity order of all equal-valued records.
items.explanation: If any ordered input failed, a threshold placed between an inverted output pair would yield a failing binary input. Exhaustive binary success rules that out. It establishes sorting, not size optimality or stable handling of record identities.
items.transfer: Explain why this implication requires a fixed min/max network rather than an arbitrary program that special-cases binary inputs.

items.prompt: The lab reports 16 of 16 binary cases sorted for a five-comparator, four-wire network. Which report keeps the evidence within its scope?
options: This is the fastest hardware sorter on every machine.
This fixed network sorts four ordered values; the lab has not measured hardware time or proved minimum size.
Any list of five comparisons must sort four values.
items.explanation: The exhaustive certificate concerns this exact ordered comparator list and wire count. The lab does not benchmark hardware, compare every smaller network, or assert a stable sort of labeled records.
items.transfer: Name a separate experiment or proof that would be needed for a performance or optimality claim.
